purpose: Separate real video-frame drops from requestVideoFrameCallback collection delay during recorded HLS 1080p60 playback.

conditions.actualHEVCOutput: libx265 Main, yuv420p, 8-bit. The API request included -10bit, but the local software FFmpeg backend produced 8-bit output.
conditions.serverSession: Exactly one encoder session for the requested quality in each run; no default-quality concurrent session.
conditions.thermal: Thermal Status 0 during the instrumented runs; no thermal throttling observed.

interpretation: H.264 accepted the expected 35964 frames over 600 seconds but Chrome dropped two frames even without per-frame collection or intermediate page evaluation.
HEVC accepted 35966 frames and dropped zero under the same counter-only conditions, so the observed H.264 drops are not explained by a general 60 Hz display or thermal limit.
The requestVideoFrameCallback count is lower than presentedFrameAdvance, so callback gaps are not one-for-one evidence of dropped video frames.

A third H.264 run observed one dropped frame at media time 950.070428 with readyState 4 and 31.393382 seconds buffered ahead. It was 1.363383 seconds from the nearest HLS segment boundary, and no HLS error occurred within two seconds. A later regeneration of the containing sequence had ideal 1501/1502 tick video PTS spacing in both the server MPEG-TS and hls.js fMP4 output; see galaxy-recorded-hls-h264-drop-segment-timestamps.json.

The follow-up profile and bitrate comparison is recorded in galaxy-recorded-hls-h264-profile-bitrate-comparison.json. Changing High to Main alone did not improve the count. Low-bitrate runs observed fewer drops, but the event count is too small to establish a reliable effect.
